def: A blood clot formed within a blood vessel or heart chamber from platelets and fibrin, which can block flow locally or break off as an embolus.
Describes chest pain that is sharp and worsens with breathing or coughing, due to irritation of the pleura. Seen in pneumonia, pulmonary embolism and pericarditis.
Movement of a limb toward the midline of the body, opposite of abduction.
A bacterial enzyme that hydrolyzes the beta-lactam ring of penicillins and cephalosporins, inactivating them. Inhibited by clavulanate, sulbactam and tazobactam.
Contractile cells surrounding secretory glands such as breast, salivary and sweat glands. They squeeze secretions into the ducts, as in milk letdown.
Membrane transport in which two substances cross in the same direction, one driving the other. Example: sodium-glucose cotransport in the proximal tubule.
Common benign breast changes in premenopausal women with cysts, fibrosis and ductal hyperplasia, causing lumpy, cyclically painful breasts.
Describes reversible narrowing of blood vessels from smooth muscle spasm, as in Prinzmetal angina and Raynaud phenomenon.
Clumps of platelets, fibrin and bacteria on heart valves in infective endocarditis. They can embolize and cause stroke or abscesses.
Located beneath the endothelial layer of a vessel. Exposed collagen here triggers platelet adhesion.
A five-carbon TCA cycle intermediate formed from isocitrate. It accepts amino groups in transamination to form glutamate.
Having a higher solute concentration than another solution; cells placed in it shrink by losing water.
Having less skin color than normal because of reduced melanin, as in vitiligo and tinea versicolor.
Increase in lens curvature to focus on near objects, driven by ciliary muscle contraction and parasympathetic input. Includes lens thickening, convergence and miosis.
Wrapped in myelin, a fatty insulating sheath that speeds conduction by saltatory transmission.
Abnormal rotation of the midgut in embryonic development, predisposing to volvulus and duodenal obstruction by Ladd bands.
Boundary in the anal canal between endoderm-derived upper part and ectoderm-derived lower part. Above it drainage is portal; below, systemic.
Drugs such as alteplase that convert plasminogen to plasmin, dissolving clots. Used in acute ischemic stroke, MI and pulmonary embolism.
Examination of the back of the eye (retina, optic disc, vessels) with an ophthalmoscope.
Low blood magnesium. Causes weakness, tremor, hypocalcemia, hypokalemia and arrhythmias such as torsades de pointes. Seen with alcoholism and loop diuretics.
Any disorder of blood clotting that causes abnormal bleeding or clotting, such as hemophilia or DIC.
Return of the membrane potential to its resting negative value after depolarization, mainly by potassium efflux.
Sensory cells that detect chemical changes, such as oxygen, carbon dioxide and pH in blood. Carotid and aortic bodies and medullary neurons regulate breathing.
Pertaining to the intima, the innermost layer of a blood vessel wall, lined by endothelium.
Tiny clots in small vessels, seen in DIC and thrombotic microangiopathies.
Toward the front end (nose) of an animal or head; in the brain, toward the forebrain.
The connective tissue layer beneath the mucosa in the gut wall, containing glands, vessels and the Meissner plexus.
A bacterium whose shape is between a coccus and a rod, such as Haemophilus, Brucella, Bordetella and Acinetobacter.
Without ovulation. Chronic anovulation causes irregular bleeding, as in PCOS.
Having normal body fluid volume, as in SIADH.
Describes processes that break down molecules to release energy, as in starvation or severe illness.
An organic acid with a ketone group, such as acetoacetate and beta-hydroxybutyrate, produced in ketoacidosis.
Dissolves readily in fats and crosses cell membranes easily; such drugs distribute widely into tissue.
Calcium deposition in damaged or necrotic tissue despite normal serum calcium, as in atheromas and damaged heart valves.
Cup-shaped structures of the kidney collecting urine from papillae and draining to the renal pelvis.
An ultra-short-acting selective beta-1 blocker given intravenously for acute control of heart rate and blood pressure.
A crackling or grating sensation or sound, felt under skin with gas or in joints with bone or cartilage rubbing.
The rate-limiting enzyme of glycolysis, converting fructose-6-phosphate to fructose-1,6-bisphosphate. Activated by AMP and fructose-2,6-bisphosphate, inhibited by ATP and citrate.
Upward movement of the foot or hand toward its top surface, as in lifting the toes toward the shin.
Thickening of the stratum corneum of the skin, as in calluses, psoriasis and actinic keratosis.
The final porphyrin precursor that receives iron via ferrochelatase to form heme. Accumulates in lead poisoning and iron deficiency.
Border regions between territories of two arteries that are most vulnerable to ischemia in hypotension. Examples: cerebral cortex between ACA/MCA, and colon splenic flexure.
Immature precursors of lymphocytes, with high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio. Seen in acute lymphoblastic leukemia.
Early set of nonspecific symptoms before a disease fully shows, such as fatigue and low-grade fever before measles rash.
Relating to Neisseria gonorrhoeae, the cause of gonorrhea.
The bony prominence at the ankle. The medial malleolus is part of the tibia and the lateral malleolus is the distal fibula.
Resembling the measles rash, with widespread small red macules and papules that merge. Common in drug eruptions.
Having a single round nucleus; mononuclear cells include lymphocytes and monocytes.
Relating to petechiae, tiny pinpoint red spots from capillary bleeding that do not blanch with pressure.
